questions.stem: Harold Brennan, 72, comes to a rural ED with a headache. It came on gradually 3 days ago, is dull, worse on the right and getting steadily worse. He takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation and is alert and oriented. What is the most important question to ask him next?
options: "Is the headache worse in the morning, or when you cough or strain?"
"Have you noticed any pain in your jaw when you chew?"
"Have you had any falls or knocks to your head in the past few weeks?"
"Do you see flashing lights or zigzag lines before the headache starts?"
questions.why: In any older person on an anticoagulant with a new, progressive headache, ask directly about falls or head injury. Patients often play down a trivial knock days earlier, and that knock is the typical story for a subdural haematoma.
notes: Raised intracranial pressure features are worth screening for, but the more urgent question is a head injury, which points straight to a subdural bleed in an anticoagulated man.
Jaw claudication screens for giant cell arteritis, which matters over 50, but a missed head injury on apixaban is far more dangerous and more likely here.
Aura points to migraine, and a first migraine at 72 is unlikely. This question will not pick up the dangerous cause in an anticoagulated man.

questions.stem: Harold, 72, has a 15 mm right subdural haematoma with 8 mm midline shift, and his GCS has fallen to 14. His last apixaban dose was at 08:00 today. CrCl is about 70 mL/min and INR is 1.2. Neurosurgical retrieval is being arranged. What is the most appropriate way to reverse his anticoagulation in this rural ED?
options: Prothrombinex-VF 50 units/kg IV, with haematology advice
questions.why: For a life-threatening bleed on a factor Xa inhibitor, give prothrombin complex concentrate (Prothrombinex-VF about 50 units/kg IV, or as per local protocol) now, with haematology advice. Use andexanet alfa where it is available and local protocol allows.
notes: Vitamin K reverses warfarin by restoring synthesis of vitamin K-dependent factors. It has no effect on apixaban, which inhibits factor Xa directly.
Idarucizumab is a specific antidote for dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor. It does not bind apixaban.
FFP does not reliably reverse apixaban, takes time to thaw and needs a large volume. Concentrated factor replacement with Prothrombinex-VF is preferred.

questions.stem: Harold, 72, takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily. His last dose was at 08:00 and his CrCl is about 70 mL/min. Bloods at 13:25 show an INR of 1.2 and an APTT of 33 s. A colleague says the anticoagulant has probably worn off. Why do these results not exclude an apixaban effect?
options: Apixaban inhibits thrombin directly, which the INR and APTT do not measure
Apixaban blocks platelet aggregation, which clotting times do not reflect
Apixaban lowers vitamin K-dependent factors only after several days of use
INR and APTT are insensitive to direct factor Xa inhibition at therapeutic levels
questions.why: Apixaban is a direct, reversible factor Xa inhibitor. Routine PT/INR and APTT reagents respond poorly to it, so they can be near normal at therapeutic levels. Only an apixaban-calibrated anti-Xa assay measures it, so judge the effect from the time of the last dose (half-life about 12 h) and renal function.
notes: Direct thrombin inhibition is how dabigatran works. Apixaban inhibits factor Xa.
Apixaban is an anticoagulant, not an antiplatelet agent. It acts on factor Xa in the coagulation cascade, not on platelet aggregation.
This describes warfarin. Apixaban works within hours of a dose and does not affect synthesis of clotting factors.

questions.stem: Harold, 72, fell 5 days ago and knocked the right side of his head. CT shows a crescent-shaped right subdural collection that crosses the suture lines, with no skull fracture. In older people, cerebral atrophy makes this kind of bleed more likely after a trivial knock. Which vessels are the most likely source?
options: Branches of the middle meningeal artery running in grooves on the inner skull
Bridging cortical veins crossing the subdural space to the dural venous sinuses
Saccular aneurysm of an artery in the subarachnoid space at the circle of Willis
Lenticulostriate perforating arteries supplying the basal ganglia and capsule
questions.why: Subdural haematoma is venous blood between the dura and the arachnoid, from torn bridging veins draining the cortex into the dural sinuses such as the superior sagittal sinus. Atrophy stretches these veins, so minor trauma can tear them. The bleed spreads along the convexity across sutures but is limited by the falx.
notes: Middle meningeal artery injury, usually with a temporal bone fracture, causes an extradural haematoma. That is lentiform and limited by the sutures, because the dura is firmly attached to them.
A ruptured berry aneurysm causes subarachnoid haemorrhage with a thunderclap onset and blood in the sulci and cisterns, not a crescentic subdural collection.
Lenticulostriate artery rupture causes a deep intracerebral haemorrhage, usually from hypertension, not an extra-axial collection after trauma.
